entities.summary:
François de Mailly (1658–1721) was a French archbishop and Cardinal who played a pivotal role in the Catholic Church's response to the Enlightenment. Born in Paris, he rose through the ranks to become Archbishop of Reims, where he oversaw the construction of a new cathedral and implemented various reforms. De Mailly's influence extended beyond his ecclesiastical duties, as he served as a key advisor to French monarchs Louis XIV and Louis XV. His legacy can be seen in the Catholic Church's continued emphasis on tradition and hierarchy in the face of modernizing forces.

De Mailly's appointment as Archbishop of Reims in 1708 marked a significant turning point in his career, as he worked to modernize the church's governance and administration. He also played a crucial role in the development of the Jesuit Order, serving as a superior of the order's French province. De Mailly's commitment to the Catholic Church's core teachings and traditions has endured long after his death, with many regarding him as a champion of orthodoxy in an era of great change.

Despite his influence, de Mailly's life was not without controversy. He was known for his conservative views on women's roles in the church and his opposition to the use of vernacular languages in worship. These views have been the subject of much debate among historians, with some viewing him as a champion of traditional values and others as a relic of a bygone era.

In the words of Cardinal de Retz, de Mailly 'was a man of great virtue, great piety, and great zeal, but also of great pride and great obstinacy.' This complex portrait of a man reflects the nuances of de Mailly's legacy, which continues to be felt in the Catholic Church's ongoing struggle to balance tradition and innovation.
